subtopic: STEVEN TRUSCOTT-ANNOUNCEMENT OF SUBMISSION TO SUPREME COURT OF CANADA

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: STEVEN TRUSCOTT-ANNOUNCEMENT OF SUBMISSION TO SUPREME COURT OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Solicitor General has kindly forwarded me a copy of the order in council in the Truscott case setting out the decision of the government, namely that the matter be submitted to the Supreme Court of Canada. The supreme court is being asked what it would have done had there been such an appeal, which was in fact denied by one judge, as I recall the circumstances.
In view of the limitations on the supreme court, even taking into consideration the fact that it may hear certain further evidence beyond that already given, does the minister
Inquiries of the Ministry not realize how very difficult, if not impossible, will be the onus resting on the appellant under the circumstances, the law and jurisprudence being what it is?

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: STEVEN TRUSCOTT-ANNOUNCEMENT OF SUBMISSION TO SUPREME COURT OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I took into consideration the representations put forward on the floor of this house by the right hon. gentleman. I might say that we gave meticulous consideration to all representations, and in my humble opinion we reached a conclusion which will meet the purpose, which is, of course, to determine whether Truscott was the victim of a miscarriage of justice. It was in an effort to reach that end that we made this reference to the supreme court.
In view of the fact that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre asked a question and received a promise on April 19, I think it would be in order for me now to place on the record the form of review. It has now been decided to refer the case to the Supreme Court of Canada pursuant to section 55 of the Supreme Court Act. The pertinent part of the order in council puts this question to the court:
Had an anneal by Steven Murray Truscott been made to the Supreme Court of Canada as is now permitted by section 597A of the Criminal Code of Canada, what disposition would the court have made of such appeal on a consideration of the existing record and such further evidence as the court, in its discretion, may receive and consider?

subtopic: STEVEN TRUSCOTT-ANNOUNCEMENT OF SUBMISSION TO SUPREME COURT OF CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, does the Solicitor General not see the difficulty here, that under the rules of the supreme court the limitations on that court are of such a nature as to practically deny any consideration of whether there has been a miscarriage of justice? The suggestion was made that the crown in its wisdom, had it come to the conclusion that there may well have been a miscarriage of justice, could grant a new trial. Would that not have been more appropriate? What were the reasons for the failure to accept that suggestion, since the supreme court has already ruled that there is no appeal.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: STEVEN TRUSCOTT-ANNOUNCEMENT OF SUBMISSION TO SUPREME COURT OF CANADA
speechtext: Order, please. I would think the question posed by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition is argumentative in nature, and I doubt very much if it should be allowed.

subtopic: STEVEN TRUSCOTT-ANNOUNCEMENT OF SUBMISSION TO SUPREME COURT OF CANADA
speechtext:
I did not want to make it argumentative, Mr. Speaker. I am trying to help in this matter. I have been concerned in these cases myself, and we all know of
April 26. 1966

Inquiries of the Ministry serious instances of the miscarriage of justice. A policeman in Montreal was acquitted the day before yesterday after being sentenced to be hanged two years ago.
Is the minister in a position to say why the government is placing the matter before the supreme court in this way, by way of consideration similar to the course followed in the Coffin case? What were the reasons why the government would not give consideration to a new trial? Did the government conclude that it was unable to do so on the basis of the evidence that had been offered?

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: STEVEN TRUSCOTT-ANNOUNCEMENT OF SUBMISSION TO SUPREME COURT OF CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, allow me to say to the right hon. gentleman with the greatest respect that there is considerable difference between the type of reference in this case and that in the Coffin matter. I would point out that this has gone beyond the usual rules relating to appeals to the Supreme Court of Canada. I would with respect draw the attention of the right hon. gentleman-I do not think I need to do so, however-to section 103, I believe it is, of the Supreme Court of Canada Act, which permits that court to make rules to deal with any reference brought before it.

subtopic: STEVEN TRUSCOTT-ANNOUNCEMENT OF SUBMISSION TO SUPREME COURT OF CANADA
speechtext: That is right.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: STEVEN TRUSCOTT-ANNOUNCEMENT OF SUBMISSION TO SUPREME COURT OF CANADA
speechtext: We took all these matters into consideration. I give the solemn assurance to the house that after long and anxious consideration we deemed that the reference in this form would be the best way to deal with the question.

subtopic: STEVEN TRUSCOTT-ANNOUNCEMENT OF SUBMISSION TO SUPREME COURT OF CANADA
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. I wonder whether the Solicitor General could say why, if it was possible under section 55 to refer directly to the supreme court the question of the innocence or guilt of Steven Truscott, the matter should not have been referred directly instead of by way of appeal, which is very limited in scope?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: STEVEN TRUSCOTT-ANNOUNCEMENT OF SUBMISSION TO SUPREME COURT OF CANADA
speechtext: Order, please. I recognize that the question which has been asked by the hon. member for Greenwood does not differ too much from the type of question asked by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition, which I considered to be argumentative to some extent. It does appear to me that we are embarking upon an exchange of views among legal experts in the house. Perhaps we might hear from the hon. member for Kamloops, who wants to ask a supplementary question, but I suggest that his question should not be argumentative.

subtopic: STEVEN TRUSCOTT-ANNOUNCEMENT OF SUBMISSION TO SUPREME COURT OF CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think you will find it is not argumentative at all but is addressed to a related factor, which is this. Did the Solicitor General or the government give consideration to the question of providing counsel to argue the matter for Steven Truscott, and paying the expenses of counsel and related expenses of investigation that are necessarily concomitant to the gathering of new evidence, the submitting of new facts and the obtaining of opinion evidence, and so on? Was this considered, and if so what decision was made as to whether the expenses of counsel in this connection should be paid?

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: STEVEN TRUSCOTT-ANNOUNCEMENT OF SUBMISSION TO SUPREME COURT OF CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am satisfied that the government will ensure that Mr. Truscott will not be handicapped by lack of funds in putting his case adequately before the court.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: STEVEN TRUSCOTT-ANNOUNCEMENT OF SUBMISSION TO SUPREME COURT OF CANADA
speechtext: May I ask one further supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Do the terms of reference as drawn make it possible for the supreme court to hear any new evidence in the case?

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: STEVEN TRUSCOTT-ANNOUNCEMENT OF SUBMISSION TO SUPREME COURT OF CANADA
speechtext: With respect, Mr. Speaker, I believe the terms of reference speak for themselves.

subtopic: STEVEN TRUSCOTT-ANNOUNCEMENT OF SUBMISSION TO SUPREME COURT OF CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Solicitor General. Can we interpret the answer the minister has just given to the hon. member for Kamloops as an assurance that the legal costs of Truscott, and the costs of assembling the evidence, will be paid by the government?

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: STEVEN TRUSCOTT-ANNOUNCEMENT OF SUBMISSION TO SUPREME COURT OF CANADA
speechtext: No request has been made for legal or financial assistance, but I can assure the hon. member that lack of funds will not stand in the way of Mr. Truscott having an adequate opportunity to present his case.

speechtext:
Can we get this
pinned down? If a request is made-

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert Winters (Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. S-23, to amend the Export and Import Permits Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, section 27 of the Export and Import Permits Act now provides that the act will expire on July 31, 1966. The purpose of the proposed amendment is to extend the act for three more years. The act in its present form came into force originally in 1954 to expire in 1957, and was extended in 1957, 1960 and 1963, in each case for another three years.
The act under section 3 provides the authority necessary for control of exports of arms, ammunition and implements of war, and also of atomic energy materials and other strategic materials, in order to ensure that these are not shipped to destinations where their use might be detrimental to the security of Canada or her allies.
The act also provides authority to control the export of materials which become in short supply in order to protect the supply position of Canadian industry. The act provides authority for control of all exports to certain countries listed in an area control list, which includes all countries in the Sino-Soviet bloc.
The act under section 5 provides authority for control of imports of a commodity which is scarce in world markets or subject to intergovernmental allocation. It also provides authority for control of imports of commodities which are under price support in Canada pursuant to acts named in the section. It also provides authority to implement an intergovernmental arrangement or commitment.
The proposed amendment is a simple renewal of the act unchanged in its provisions. These provisions were debated in the Senate on March 29, 1966, during the second reading and discussed in detail in the banking and commerce committee at that time.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister has given us a brief outline of the importance of this act and has indicated that the amendment will be simply an extension of the act for a three year period. Under those circumstances the house could assume that this might be done in very short order but, though we may deal with it expeditiously, nevertheless
April 26. 1966

we should take a look at the act because it was not discussed at any great length three years ago.
For those who may be discussing this act three years from now and who have the good sense to look at the Hansard index to find out what was said on this occasion, I shall list for their advantage something I would have appreciated myself on this occasion, namely, certain references which are helpful to a review of the act. I suggest that anyone wishing to make a survey of the act might look back to Hansard of March 16, 1954, page 3065 and following pages, where there is a good indication of the modifications made to the act on that occasion and also a listing of the strategic materials that were then indicated as being prohibited from shipment to various countries of the world.
The second Hansard reference I give is March 5, 1957, starting at page 1903. On that occasion there was extended discussion. The history of the act was given at some length by the then parliamentary secretary, Mr. Dickey, who was followed by Hon. Donald Fleming, then opposition critic of the Department of Trade and Commerce who, at page 1906 and following pages, also gave an extensive review of the act.
The third reference I give is May 17, 1960, page 3963, when the act was again extended for a three year period and was piloted through the house by my parliamentary secretary of that time, Mr. Pallett, with the chief critic from the then opposition being the present Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mcllraith).
In 1963, when the act again came up for renewal, the amendment was passed without debate. There were certain circumstances obtaining at that time which induced us to push through the act without giving it complete consideration. The government house leader of that time, now the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill), was floundering a little and, as I usually do when the house is in difficulty, I came to his assistance and we passed the act in a few minutes thus helping him out. There was no debate and consequently the 1963 reference will be of no advantage to anyone examining the act in the future.
However, anyone interested in the history of the act will be repaid by glancing at the 1957 debate. I do not intend on this occasion to give an extensive summary of the act. I simply point out that it is six years since it has been discussed and perhaps the house
Export and Import Permits Act should take a look at it to see how advantageous it is and whether it should be continued in its present form.
In the debate in 1954 Hon. Donald Fleming and Hon. J. M. Macdonnell criticized the government of that day for its avid desire for power. They thought the act was continuing in the hands of the government more power than was desirable. In 1957 the discussion ran in a somewhat similar vein and it was suggested by the opposition of that period, the Conservative party, that possibly the act need not be continued.
In 1960, when the positions had been reversed, the Minister of Public Works, then in opposition, took the stand that perhaps the act was no longer required. So it is obvious that people change their opinions when they cross the floor of the house.
Originally the act was designed to be used in emergencies. It was a carryover from some of the wartime legislation. When it was revised in 1954 the Korean problem was causing quite a bit of difficulty and so the act had a purpose for emergency situations. Then the act was continued after that time to make provision for problems that could arise due to the scarcity of certain commodities, either on the export or import side, and it had an additional, important purpose, to prevent the export of strategic materials to sensitive areas in the world where trouble might break out. In other words, the act prevents the export of arms, ammunition and base metals that might be useful for war purposes.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
On the import side it has not been used as extensively as on the export side but it has been used in order to protect agriculture and fisheries in this country on occasions when it appeared that the market was going to be flooded with commodities which were in good supply in Canada and in the hope that the price level for the producer in Canada would be maintained.
When we reach the committee stage of the bill perhaps the minister could provide us with some details with regard to the operation of this act in recent years. On one occasion in 1954 I believe the act was referred to the Standing Committee on Banking and Commerce. I do not suggest that be done on this occasion because that committee has perhaps enough work to do without having an additional bill put in front of it. However, the convenience in doing so is that the officials could appear before that committee
April 26. 1966

Export and Import Permits Act to give full information on the operation of the act. Perhaps, however, we can obtain sufficient information today from the minister when we are in the committee stage.
I should like to know how extensively the act is being used at the present time, the total of export permits over the last two years, for example, and similarly the total of import permits for that period, also the type of goods affected on either the export side or the import side. Perhaps the minister might have this information available for us when the time comes.
Then I wish to deal briefly with one other aspect of this act. It was never intended for purposes other than those which I have indicated on the export and on the import side. Recently it has been used for the application of sanctions against Southern Rhodesia. When we were debating the subject of Southern Rhodesia in January and February I dealt at some length with this particular aspect of the matter. I wondered whether the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) was making use of this act for a purpose which never was intended when the act was introduced and when it was modified over the years. There was no suggestion in any of the debates of the past that this act would be used for the imposition of sanctions.
The imposition of sanctions, of course, is one step closer to the imposition of force and you get into very dangerous waters when that is done. When we were discussing this matter with the Secretary of State for External Affairs I suggested that the action at that time should have taken the form of presenting to the house a resolution asking for the approval of the action of the government with regard to Southern Rhodesia. Instead of so doing he made use of this act, with the co-operation of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters), to impose sanctions. As I said, from the history of the act, which I do not wish to review at too great length, it never was intended for that purpose; it was intended to prevent the export of strategic materials to sensitive areas of the world where warfare might break out. Naturally Canada does not wish to be involved in anything of that nature or be a party to assisting any country or any groups who are about to engage or are engaged in warfare. So the limitation on strategic materials, was imposed for a very definite purpose and of course should be maintained.
On the commodity side, in our interest as a world trader we have endeavoured not to

place any restraints in the way of our manufacturers and exporters in the shipping of non-strategic materials abroad. On the import side the use of the act up to the present, so far as I am aware, has been only on occasion when there was a really serious threat to producers in this country. Now, however, we have reached a stage where the act is used as a political arm for the purpose of applying sanctions involving a restriction of trade between Canada and Rhodesia, a restriction of trade in order to compel Rhodesia to take some political action of which Canada approves. Canada expresses its approval of that political action by saying in effect to Rhodesia, we will not trade with you any longer; we will cut off the export of goods to you and the import of goods from you in order to cripple your economy, if we can do so, to the point where you will revise the political situation in your country.
I do not know that the Minister of Trade and Commerce can deal with this particular problem, although he has to carry some of the responsibility, and I realize it overlaps into the field of external affairs. The Minister of Trade and Commerce, however, is the person who is responsible to parliament for the application of this act; he is the one who has to sign the export and import permits and supervise the act. At the same time, as Minister of Trade and Commerce he is responsible for the promotion of export and import trade. Therefore he is rather caught in a vise and has to renounce his good offices as a person in favour of expansion of trade to accommodate the Secretary of State for External Affairs who wishes to apply pressure to a country within the commonwealth for purposes to which this government has given consent.
When the Minister of Trade and Commerce replies, I hope he will give us a little advice with regard to this particular problem. When we reach the committee stage I will ask him one or two specific questions. To give him a little warning I should like to ask him now, and he can reply later, whether the extension of our embargo involving the application of sanctions to Southern Rhodesia was discussed with the continuing committee of NATO with whom 1 believe we are supposed to discuss any alterations in the lists of prohibited articles which come under the jurisdiction of the Department of Trade and Commerce in administering this particular act. Has there been a discussion with the members of NATO with regard to the extension of embargoes
April 26, 1966

under the Export and Import Permits Act or have we just been going it alone?
The other question which emerges is in reference to the statement the minister made that certain action can be taken by way of intergovernmental agreement. The intergovernmental agreement between the United Kingdom and Canada concerning Rhodesia, it seems to me, has been rather carelessly expressed in the letters which were exchanged between the two countries. I am wondering whether the Minister of Trade and Commerce is relying entirely on that or is he now placing some reliance upon the action of the Security Council of the United Nations.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
I conclude by saying that I think the Export and Import Permits Act serves a useful purpose when it is restricted to those things for which it was designed, the prevention of the export of strategic materials to sensitive areas of the world, and restricting imports when there is some danger to the producers of this country. I do not think it was ever intended, or should be used, for the imposition of sanctions.

Export and Import Permits Act before we reach the committee stage I should like to mention certain things about the act which, after reading it, might cause one to wonder. The act on its surface appears to be very powerful, giving very wide and uncontrolled discretionary powers to the minister. Mr. Chairman, we are pleased to have this increase in the capital and borrowing capacity of the Farm Credit Corporation because the expenses of farmers are higher than ever before in the history of Canada. When we speak about $1 billion in lending capacity in respect of the Farm Credit Corporation we are speaking of something which a few years ago was not applicable. We did not expect that the Farm Credit Corporation would have to have $1 billion available for the many farmers across the country. However, times have changed considerably.
While I was home over the Easter recess I noticed that some of the land which had been sold by farmers had been sold for amounts which nobody ever expected. For instance, an ordinary, good farm comprising half a section of land had been sold for $45,000. I well remember the years when I bought my first half section of land. At that time the price was $5,000 and it was a very high price to pay. So times have changed.
This increase will help place the farmers in a position to avail themselves of larger amounts to buy land through borrowing from the Farm Credit Corporation. But what, about the farmer who is starting out, the young farmer who is perhaps not able to take on where the old man left off? He wishes to go on farming the same as his father, his grandfather and others of his family have done in the past. I think there must be some other solution to the problems of the young farmer. As I said yesterday, there is the high cost of farm machinery and the high cost of living. This applies, of course, to every Canadian citizen.
However, I should like to impress the minister with the fact that there is another side to the picture. The farmer needs not only the opportunity to borrow large amounts of money through the Farm Credit Corporation but also must be placed in a position where he can repay the amounts he borrows from the corporation. This applies to all farmers from the west to the east.
Again I should like to stress the second point I emphasized yesterday under other circumstances, that is, that the Minister of Agriculture must take steps to improve the income of the farmer so that he will be in a position to be able to repay these loans.

Mr. Chairman, the legislation before us has been anticipated for some time. The proposed increase in the authorized capital of the Farm Credit Corporation from $24 million to $40 million will increase the lending capacity of the corporation and thereby increase the borrowing authorization from $600 million to $1 billion. This is all related to the changes now taking place in the agricultural industry.
The transition that is now taking place in the farming industry is causing an obvious trend toward larger operations. This change in the method or mode of farming has some obviously desirable features but I say with certainty that there are a number of undesirable features as well.
It would not be necessary to increase the amount of loan capital available to the Farm Credit Corporation if we had a better agricultural prices program in this country. Agricultural prices and farm incomes are not
Farm Credit Act
as high as they should be in relation to our economy. For this reason I believe it is incumbent upon the government to do something to increase the amount of farm credit available. Governments at the federal and provincial level have been increasing the amount of credit capital available to farmers and there has been a steady though not alarming increase in debt on the part of farm operators.
Since it is a fact that our agricultural pricing mechanism is deficient and inadequate, we are not in a position to oppose an increase in farm credit. But we certainly want to say that we have some misgivings in this regard because this is a poor substitute for proper pricing and increased income.

In addition to the plea made by the hon. member for Oxford, I ask the government to give consideration to the easing of the requirements under the Farm Credit Act. I realize there must be some limitation because if prudence were not exercised the corporation would find itself in a position of extending loans without security and with little likelihood of repayment. One of the greatest problems-here I agree with the hon. member for Oxford and the hon. member for Springfield and I believe the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale also mentioned this-is that we need to be even more concerned about finding ways and means of seeing that farmers have an opportunity to repay these loans. I know that an increasing number of well-established farmers are today getting into financial difficulty and have been for the last two or three years because of the so-called cost-price squeeze.
Every time land, capital investment or the price of farm machinery goes up substantially without a corresponding increase in the farmer's receipts, the cost-price squeeze, of course, becomes even more acute. Therefore I am not in full agreement at the moment that the ceiling per individual application should be raised so soon after the last increase which, as I said, was 100 per cent. Having said that, Mr. Chairman, I fully realize that the capital investment for a farm large enough to produce a reasonable standard of living continues to go up and up and up. Therefore we have to bear in mind that it now takes $50,000, $60,000 or $70,000 of capital investment in land, machinery, livestock and so on for a farmer to have sufficient production to provide a reasonably adequate standard of living.
The situation is perhaps not so difficult for well established farmers who have accumulated the necessary capital, but it is extremely difficult for a young farmer to obtain this amount of capital. If the young farmer does not obtain the capital he is unable to obtain the productivity necessary to provide a reasonable standard of living; his net income is not sufficient.

Second, in my riding, loans were refused several times under total loan No. 3. To qualify, the farmer must not be over 45 years of age.
Now, I would ask the minister to bring this fact to the attention of the corporation to determine whether it would not be possible to extend the age limit to 50 years. On account of this, we are losing good farmers who have operated small units for some years, but who, because they are refused a loan to enable them to earn their livelihood, are forced to leave their farms.
April 26, 1966

Another point I should like to bring to the attention of the minister concerns the maximum which was increased two years ago from $22,500 to $27,500. To my mind, a small increase to $35,000 at 5 per cent interest would be desirable, in view of the recent amendments to the act. As a result, a larger number of farmers could qualify for a loan. I think this is the only way a farmer can obtain money to settle on a farm. Nobody lends money to farmers nowadays, except the Farm Credit Corporation. It is desirable to improve the act so as to enable the majority of farmers to benefit from it.
Aware of the good sense of the Minister of Agriculture-I believe that his riding is similar to my own riding of Glengarry-Prescott and that the problems I am bringing to his attention have already been brought home to him by the farmers of his own riding-I shall rely on him to intervene with the corporation so as to solve these problems satisfactorily.

Expressing another opinion, the hon. member for Springfield told us that in his opinion the loan ceiling might be lowered. I believe one important factor was overlooked by those putting forward arguments in favour of both a higher and a lower figure, namely, the, fact that the staff which serves the Farm Credit Corporation is made up of extremely able and dedicated civil servants. This has been shown throughout the years. In other words, regardless of the ceiling the loan has to be based on a good background. Otherwise no loan is made, and that is all there is to it. It does not matter whether the application is well below the ceiling or above it. The field staff take a look at all applications and deal with them promptly and efficiently.
In the Okanagan I had occasion within the last ten days to listen to the manager of the Farm Credit Corporation for the province of British Columbia, as did a number of extraordinarily good orchardists, and we were
Farm Credit Act
all exceedingly pleased with the manner in which he explained the corporation, its aims and objectives, and how applications were handled. He satisfied us with his well prepared speech and with the easy and able answers he gave to all questions, no matter how difficult. Incidentally, in that area many of the questions were difficult because many applications have had to be turned down.
The reason I am stressing this is that with the growth of farm units in Canada over the last number of years, with the increased cost of farm machinery, so ably stressed by the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale, and the resulting increased capital that has to be put into a farm, it may well be necessary for the minister to examine the question of increasing the maximum amount of loans that can be made. The hon. member for Oxford emphasized the dairy industry as one requiring exceedingly large capital to finance it. No doubt this will be pointed out to the minister by his staff.
But once again I would point out that no matter what maximum is fixed, and I believe the present maximum is a fairly good one, the staff of the Farm Credit Corporation are not going to turn all the money loose and say: Farmers, come and get it. They will ask what kind of units farmers have, the purpose for which they require the money, and then with their experience in all fields they will help them.
From its inception the corporation and its method of making loans have been far superior to the old farm loan board. The statute was introduced by a Conservative government and it is one of the better ones we have in Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I have just a few words to say about the Farm Credit Corporation which was set up by the previous government and which on the whole has worked very well. I am all in favour of increasing the amount of money. This is absolutely necessary in the high cost, high production age in which we are living, with the high cost of buildings, machinery and equipment.
One thing which concerns me is that it appears to be much harder for a small farmer to get a loan than a big farmer. I know a few cases in point. I shall not go into detail on them but one in particular, a dairy farm, seems big enough to me to be able to guarantee the loan sought. The buildings and equipment are good for half the loan and the land without the buildings is almost worth the

April 26, 1966
Farm Credit Act
other half. I wonder whether there is a tendency to go against the small farmer because of his smaller productivity and not take into account the help he receives from his family growing up on his farm.
On big farms there is the labour factor involving the cost of wages but in the particular case I have in mind the farmer does not have to employ any labour at all and so has a terrific advantage. I ask the minister to examine this point. Surely we want to keep our young boys and girls on the farms in rural Canada. Surely we do not want to discriminate against the small operator if his productivity is sound. Mistakes have been made in this regard and I think I can prove the point. A small farmer with a milk contract and family help can have an economic unit.
The milk of human kindness should be showered upon the small farmer. Otherwise he is the fellow for whom we will have to dig into our purses in order to rehabilitate him when he moves off his land. We will have to buy his land when we should be trying to keep him on it.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, first of all, I wish to thank hon. members who, with their constructive and valuable contributions, have helped me in respect of the suggestions they have made with regard to the administration of the act. On behalf of the officials of the Farm Credit Corporation I also acknowledge the pleasing comments made by members on all sides about the efficiency of their administration. There were one or two specific questions which did not involve policy and which I might answer. Though there were many suggestions in the policy area with which I might personally agree, needless to say questions of policy are a matter of cabinet responsibility.
The question was asked what size the fund would have to be in order to become a self-sufficient revolving one. I believe it was the hon. member for Macleod who asked that question. At the present time 27 per cent of the funds that are available for lending come from repayments by farmers. The rest comes from additional capital such as that which we are providing here. The officials of my department estimate that the fund will become a fully self-sustaining revolving fund when it is in the neighbourhood of $2 billion. I am not actuarially sure of this figure but it is the best estimate my officials can give.
[Mr. Rynard.l
The hon. member for Macleod also asked a question with regard to that part of the repayment bearing an open interest rate rather than the fixed rate, in other words, in relation to the excess above $20,000 under Part II and above $27,500 under Part III. The rate has to be approved by the governor in council and now is approved at 6f per cent which I think is probably under the market in most other areas but certainly is above the 5 per cent paid on the first portion of the loan.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
Useful suggestions have been made from all s-des of the house. May I say that since my term of office as Minister of Agriculture commenced I certainly have been most fortunate in receiving co-operation from all sides of the house, not on a partisan basis but apparently in all cases because of what hon. members felt was in the best interest of the farming community. I may say this is something which has been most heartwarming and encouraging. Not only in respect of this house where I would expect to find that kind of co-operation but also in working with the provincial departments of agriculture and provincial organizations I may say that universally I have found this same spirit. All persons engaged in public life, both at the political level or at the level of public service, provincially and federally, seem very anxious to work in the best interest of the agricultural community.
At no time have I had any impediment in doing my job because of anyone acting in a partisan rather than a public spirited way on behalf of the farmers. If I do not succeed in doing an adequate or satisfactory job on behalf of the agricultural community, certainly I will have no cause for complaint that it was because of lack of co-operation or lack of good will on the part of persons of other political stamp who are involved in the problems of agriculture. I do wish to thank hon. members not only for their co-operation in respect of this bill but also for the very valuable help and the suggestions I have received from them at all times in respect of agricultural problems.
I was extremely interested to hear sugges-t'ons such as that with regard to the partnership aspect and the possibility of increasing the loans in respect of partnerships. I said earlier that family corporations now are eligible for loans. Off the top of my head may I say I really am not familiar with whether the loan is increased by reason of the corporation
April 26. 1966

aspect. To the best of my knowledge I think that while a family corporation is eligible for a loan it is eligible only for the present maximum loan which an individual could obtain.
If I understood it correctly, I think the suggestion made by several hon. members was that partnerships and family corporations should have available to them larger loans because of the number of persons or the number of families involved, the size of the holding and the number of viable agricultural units which would comprise that holding. I shall be very interested to look into this aspect of the matter because I think these are very worth-while suggestions.
I was also very interested to hear of the concern of hon. members with regard to young people going into farming and the availability of more ready capital and the possibility of making farms available to them by means of a lower down payment through greater flexibility in the Farm Credit Corporation. I believe the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott (Mr. Ethier) very forcefully made that point. I think this is a very worth-while matter and one we should look into. I think all of us are somewhat concerned by the fact that the incidence of older people is more prevalent in farming than it is in other fields of economic endeavour in our country. It is very difficult for a young man to get started in farming, possibly by reason of the cost-price squeeze which has been referred to so forcefully by hon. members.
It is possible that young people have not found it too attractive to go into farming in past years. Surely if our farm economy is to be sound we must do everything we can to encourage young people to enter the agricultural sector of our economy. I shall be very pleased to look into this aspect of the suggestion made by hon. members.

I agree with the purposes of the bill now before us. The Minister now lauds this bill and urges us to accept it so that by unanimous consent it can be given third reading and passed. I have no objection to that procedure because of the merit of the proposal but I do submit that it is in effect a contribution to the inflationary trend. We will be putting more money into the hands of the people who will borrow under this act, giving them greater purchasing power, which undoubtedly they will use and thereby pumping more money into circulation and contributing to any potential inflation. That is exactly the spectre the minister says is confronting him.
Several things have happened in recent days which I wish to point out. The position taken regarding the extension to the Prince Rupert grain elevator, when compared to the purposes of the present bill, creates an illogical situation. Farm Credit Act
would contribute to inflation. It seems to me that he cannot have it both ways.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, some of us are rather disturbed about the incorporation of the proposed bank. In the initial presentation two or three years ago the proponents of the bank engaged in a little misleading propaganda in order to try to convince those who might just look at the surface that the bank would be publicly owned. I do not mean publicly owned in the sense of government ownership but owned by members of the general public as distinct from ownership by corporate entities.
The proponents of the bill exhibited this tendency to propagandize by setting out in the bill of previous years the names of sundry individuals who were listed as shareholders. The names of those individuals covered two pages of the bill introduced at that time. Together with the names of the individuals who were listed as shareholders was a designation of their profession. We find listed in the bill a number of people who were classified as persons from what we might call

April 26. 1966
Private Bills
the ordinary walk of life. Architects, solicitors, a couple of executives, farmers, physicians, a professor and an investment dealer were listed and I think they even had a blacksmith listed at one stage. I shall not read the names and occupations of the individuals listed in the previous bills and classified as the major shareholders except to say there were about 100 of them.
Inasmuch as these names and professions were contained in the first clause of the bill presented to us at that time, I submit it was designed to leave the impression that here was a true people's bank, that not only was it to be a bank dedicated to the advancement of banking interests in western Canada with its headquarters in Winnipeg but it would also be owned and controlled by the common people.
In the bill before us at the present time those who will control the Bank of Western Canada have dropped that subterfuge and list in clause 1 merely the names of a few top flight individuals, namely, James Elliott Coyne, executive; Sinclair McKnight Stevens, solicitor; Maxwell Bruce, one of Her Majesty's counsel, all of the city of Toronto in the province of Ontario. Then there is listed one Edward Rex Plewman Nesbitt, executive, of the city of Winnipeg in the province of Manitoba, and John Leslie Bodie, executive, of the city of Edmonton in the province of Alberta, followed by the words, "together with such persons as become shareholders in the corporation by this act created, are, incorporated under the name Bank of Western Canada hereinafter called 'the Bank.' "
I say that the subterfuge of broad participation by people has been dropped and we see that of the five individuals listed, who incidentally shall be the provisional directors, three come from the city of Toronto, one from Winnipeg and one from Edmonton. The names and occupations of common people have been dropped. I think it is a little more honest to do it this way than was the case previously.
I believe some consideration should be given to the manner in which this bank is effectively owned or controlled. The proceedings of the Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs Committee which considered the bill and dealt with it in some detail-in fact the detail ranged over the period of three or four sittings-show the extent to which the proposed Bank of Western Canada is owned and controlled by other than common people. I might say that the information was not easy

to obtain. I was not on the committee and was not able to attend its hearings, but a reading of the evidence and the information elicited by such individuals as the member for Lapointe, the member for Acadia and others who asked searching questions of the witnesses indicates that it was difficult to obtain full information about the company.
In the Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence No. 1 of the Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs Committee there are extensive references stretching over quite a number of pages which show that the ownership or effective control of the Bank of Western Canada is by way of quite a bit of involvement with other companies. Perhaps I could read briefly from page 14 of the proceedings. Mr. Stevens was giving evidence and pointed out the following with regard to raising the money for the bank:
[DOT]	(6:20 p.m.l
This money was originally raised in February and March, 1964 and is broken down as follows: first, over 5,000 people placed $6,450,000 in trust with the Canada Permanent Trust Company for future investment in the proposed bank.
One might think 5,000 people would constitute a broadly based ownership of a company such as this. Then he said:
Second, a further 2,000 people put in trust $3,750,000 to be invested by the Wellington Financial Corporation in the proposed bank.
We will have more to say about the Wellington Financial Corporation in a moment.
A further 2,600 people bought shares in Canadian Finance and Investment, which in turn is committed to investing $2,250,000 in the proposed bank.
We will also have more to say about Canadian Finance and Investment in a moment.
I should have mentioned that Wellington is a Toronto based company originally established in Guelph, Ontario, in 1926. The Canadian Finance and Investment is a Winnipeg based company originally established in 1926 in that city. The York Trust and Savings Corporation of Toronto is committed to investing $495,000 in the bank, and the proposed provisional directors of the bank are committed to a further $37,500.
This statement was followed by extensive questioning as will be seen from a perusal of pages 14 to at least 32 and subsequent pages as well. I am just going as far as page 32 because I think the gist of the ownership is shown there. There are some rather involved answers given to questions asked by the hon. member for Lapointe. Finally Mr. Stevens,
April 26, 1966

the witness, answered some of these questions as follows:
The bank will be owned by four different main groups. The first group is a group which owns shares directly in the bank and are now holding trustee certificates. Now, all together they number a total of about 5,100 odd. The next largest shareholder in the bank will be the Wellington Financial Corporation, which owns approximately 30 per cent of the proposed bank.
We know, as a result of studies made by people concerned about the ownership of corporations, that a 30 per cent ownership of a corporation in the hands of one group or one individual can be used to control rather effectively the operations and activities of that particular company. Here we have the Wellington Financial Corporation, one of the companies which Mr. Stevens said was going to put some money into the bank, owning about 30 per cent of the proposed bank.
Then there were some questions put by the hon. member for Acadia. He asked Mr. Stevens about his connections with Wellington Financial Corporation, about his connections with Canadian Finance and Investments Limited and his connection with York Trust and Savings Corporation. These three corporations are involved in one way or another with the proposed Bank of Western Canada. Mr. Stevens answered these queries by saying he was president of all three corporations. The hon. member for Acadia then went on to ask about another corporation, and I am quoting from page 30 of the evidence:
What is your connection with British International Financial (Canada) Limited?

speechtext:
I am also president of that company.
There follow extensive questions and answers which eventually elicited the information that the large shareholder, British International Financial (Canada) Limited, through some of the companies it controls, has absolute or effective control of this bank. We find that British International Financial (Canada) Limited will own the Bank of Western Canada directly or indirectly to the extent of almost 50 per cent.
The hon. member for Acadia put this question directly to Mr. Stevens:
Would I be right in assuming that you would have nearly 50 per cent of the paid in capital of the $13 million in this proposed chartered bank?

This provision should preclude the possibility of any one, single financial group or company being able to control such a corporation. I gather from reading Mr. Stevens' remarks that he really is not in favour of effective control of the Bank of Western Canada. He would like to see a situation prevail in which there was a wide distribution of ownership. He would like to see the Bank of Western Canada owned and controlled by individual shareholders and he would be happy if some authority in government would come along and tell him subsequent to the passage of this measure, if it ever is passed, that is what he has to do.

Mr. Chairman, in rising to take part in this debate I want to say at the outset that I have been greatly interested in banks in Canada for a number of years. I have followed the applications of several of the banks which have been before this house and the other place over the last
IMr. Howard I
two years. I have become particularly interested in this bank for the reason that it is proposed to call it the Bank of Western Canada, which immediately arouses interest in western Canada.
I am one of those who believe in free enterprise. I believe that in competition with one another under the free enterprise system the greatest savings can be made and the greatest efficiency brought about. I think the same theory holds true with regard to banks. Therefore, basically I am all for more banks in Canada.
On the other hand, as a member of parliament I feel that the right to be granted and to operate a bank charter is a great privilege. I do not think that I or other members of parliament should take our office lightly and grant a charter to anybody who may want to apply for one. It is our duty to examine every applicant and to make certain first of all that he is worthy of the charter, second, that he is capable of carrying it out and, third, that he will be sincere, once he has obtained the charter, in working for the general advantage of Canada. I do not expect him to lose money or to take money out of his own pocket to foster, promote, or continue to promote, a bank of which he holds the charter. But I do believe that in operating a bank in Canada under a charter which has been granted by parliament the operator should work for the general advantage of Canada along with making a profit for himself, though perhaps a limited one.
I believe that a bank charter is something similar to a licence to operate a public utility. It is similar to the right to transport oil or gas across Canada as in the case of Interprovincial Pipe Line or Trans-Canada Pipe Line. They have the charters to move oil or gas across Canada. We have also set up a National Energy Board to make certain that the monopoly we have granted them is controlled and will work for the general advantage of Canada. This is why I examined the proposed application for this charter to the best of my ability in the committee.
I am in no way opposed to the creation of more banks in Canada, but I want to establish first the three principles which I think are important and which I should like to repeat. First of all, the applicants must be worthy. In other words, they must accept the responsibility which this house places upon them with a great deal of care, sincerity and dedication. Second, they must also be capable. In other words, though you and I, Mr. April 26, 1966

Chairman, may not be capable of operating a chain of banks across Canada under a charter there are financiers who are capable of doing so. Third, they must be prepared to operate a banking system in Canada which works for the general advantage of Canada, not solely for the general advantage of themselves. These are the three basic principles upon which my questioning was founded and upon which I shall continue to question this particular application.
I am not going to quote from the committee proceedings; I want to deal in generalities. We have an application before us for a bank charter to set up a bank with a capitalization of $25 million. Money has been obtained in trust to the tune of something like $13 million. How has that money been appropriated? Under my criterion that a bank charter should work for the general advantage of Canada, if I alone were granted such a charter I would be more inclined to work for the general advantage of myself because this venture would perhaps be my sole interest. But the general application of my thinking is that the broader based the applicant, the greater the possibility he will continue to work for the advantage of different segments of industry and different parts of the economy of the country. I place a great deal of importance on the fact that such a charter as this should work for the general advantage of Canada and that the applicant should be broadly based, therefore enabling him to work to a greater degree for the general advantage of Canada.
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
When I was examining this matter initially I was greatly concerned because we were told in committee that the applicants had put up something like $6 million or more to be placed in trust in the event of the charter being awarded and that this amount had been quickly taken up by shareholders in eastern and western Canada, most of them in western Canada. We also found that the greater portion of the $13 million was controlled by finance houses owned or controlled by three individuals in Toronto. I said in the committee and I say again to this house: If 50 per cent of the amount they wanted to raise was quickly taken up by proposed shareholders in this bank, why did they not let out a little more? Why did they not let out 70 per cent? The remain'ng 30 per cent would still provide for effective control of any company. But they wanted to make sure of absolute control by retaining 51 per cent, 52 per cent or 53 per
Private Bills
cent. This raised some doubt in my mind whether these people were prepared to work for the general advantage of Canada or for the general advantage of themselves.
Consider the title of this bank-the Bank of Western Canada. We were told in committee that western Canada is a deposit surplus area. I would not have believed it. I would have thought that we westerners were spending every nickel we get. But the highest banking officials in Canada including a former governor of the Bank of Canada tell us they believe western Canada to be a deposit surplus area. With this in mind we must consider the fact that 53 per cent is to be owned and controlled in the city of Toronto and that something like 20 per cent of that 53 per cent is owned by trust and finance companies in eastern Canada. Then we should ask: Who will benefit? Where is western Canada's deposit surplus likely to go?
I am not a man who is suspicious by nature. I may be a born optimist. But when I link these two things together I have a tendency to become suspicious. It may be said that finance houses and trust companies are institutions of which many people are suspicious to begin with. I do not think I can be classified in that group. But throughout these proceedings I asked questions in an attempt to set aside the fears which were evidently in my mind with regard to the present application. At no time were these fears set aside by the witnesses.
It is well known that in the course of this summer parliament will have to deal with the Bank Act. Consideration of amendments to this legislation has been postponed for two years. Why should this application not wait until the Bank Act has been dealt with. This would clear up the doubt about foreign ownership and about the limitation on the interest rate. We would know how this application would fit into the new Bank Act. We would also know whether or not the applicants are trying to take advantage of the situation in which we find ourselves today in Canada where those granted bank charters may charge interest only up to a maximum rate of 6 per cent. In other words, they may want to get in while the going is good and then, should the maximum committee interest rate be increased to 7 per cent, they would be in a position to take advantage of it.

I am aware of that. Statements of that kind were made time and time again in the committee. I do not believe these people should not make a profit. I believe in making a profit. I know that all the banks now operating in Canada believe in making a profit. They always have from me, and I know this is really their basic interest. But by operating a network of banks across Canada they also work to the advantage of the public generally.
[DOT] (6:50 p.m.)
In this application we have to examine whether the intent is to serve the advantage of the public. If that intent is not present then parliament will be making a terrible mistake in granting these people their charter solely because we need more banks in Canada and this is one of the applications for a new bank charter. We may have 25 other applicants next year.
To me a charter to operate a bank is a privilege. It is a privilege to get into the banking business, a privilege we should not grant lightly to operate a monopoly under certain controls and rigid confinement. We must examine whether or not the applicants are worthy and whether or not they are efficient.
From my examination of the efficiency of the applicants, I would say that, if they can operate as many trust and finance companies as they do and remain in business as long as some of these companies have, they must be reasonably efficient and qualify in that respect. But for the present I am not examining them on that basis at all. I am examining whether they are worthy and will work for the general advantage of Canada. They have

not proven themselves to me on either point, and these two points are closely linked.
Are these applicants worthy? To prove worthiness they must prove desire and intent. Time and time again I questioned them in the committee. Time and time again I wanted them to say that they believed the banking system in Canada was similar to a public utility but they never did. Time and time again I wanted them to say that they were prepared to let more shareholders in but they said no.
The interesting thing in this case is that from the first time these people applied for a bank charter until this day, instead of showing evidence of where they have dispersed some of their holdings the three people involved gave evidence before the committee which convinced me that they had taken it upon themselves to gobble up more of the outstanding shares being held in trust to establish the bank. They admitted quite frankly that western Canada had quickly bought up the shares released from trust where they had been placed for the establishment of the bank. But if this is so, why did they not release more? Why did they have to keep absolute control? These are questions upon which they have failed to answer fully and conclusively in order to convince me that I should wholeheartedly endorse their application. I want to do so. I want to be on record as supporting more banks in Canada, but I take my job here seriously and I want to examine all applicants to make sure that they wish to work for the general advantage of Canada and not just for themselves.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: IMPLEMENTATION OF AGREEMENT BETWEEN" CANADA AND UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill, as its title indicates, is to give legislative effect to the recently signed income tax agreements with the United Kingdom and with Sweden. For convenience the bill is divided into two parts, the first dealing with the new agreement with the United Kingdom signed last December, and the second dealing with the supplementary agreement signed last January that amends the agreement signed with Sweden in 1951. In substance the bill is similar to the bills implementing income tax agreements or supplementary income tax agreements between Canada and other countries that have been approved by the house since 1942. Canada now has in force 12 comprehensive income tax agreements-with the United States of America, New Zealand, France, Sweden, Ireland, Denmark, West Germany, the Union of South Africa, the Netherlands, Australia, Finland and Japan.
Part I of the bill approves and gives the force of law to the agreement with the United Kingdom, which is set out in schedule 1. This agreement is considerably less comprehensive than the agreements to which I have just referred, although like them, its object is to avoid double taxation, or to reduce taxation, of the income received by individuals and corporations of one of the countries from sources in the other country. It is an interim agreement limited to four classes of income on which action could be taken pending consideration of the forthcoming report of the Royal Commission on Taxation and appraisal of the consequences for tax agreements of the recent major changes in the British tax system. Since the agreement is of an interim nature it may be terminated by either government giving six months notice, but both governments have expressed the hope that it will be replaced by, or expanded into, a comprehensive agreement as soon as this is feasible.
Hon. members will recall that the former income tax agreement between Canada and the United Kingdom signed in 1946 was terminated in accordance with its terms when Canada gave notice of termination in June 1964. This was after negotiations, held over a three year period with a view to amending

the agreement in accordance with Canadian policy, had proved unsuccessful. The main point of difference leading to the termination of the old agreement was the fact that it prevented Canada from imposing any tax on dividends paid by a wholly owned subsidiary in Canada to its parent company in Britain.
The new agreement establishes a general rule, similar to that in other Canadian tax agreements, that all pensions and annuities will be taxable only in the country where the recipient of the pension or annuity is a resident. This differs from the old agreement in which the rule was that pensions paid in respect of British or Canadian governmental or military services could be taxed only in the country of source.
There are exceptions to the new general rule that preserve the position that persons in receipt of such governmental pensions had under the old agreement, if they prefer to retain that position. The provisions of the agreement concerning the tax treatment of recipients of pensions will benefit some 15,000 Canadian residents receiving pensions from United Kingdom sources and some 2,500 recipients of Canadian pensions living in Britain whose financial position has been affected by the termination of the old agreement.
The other classes of income with which the agreement deals are profits of an enterprise earned by a permanent establishment, for example a branch office, profits from the operation of ships or aircraft, and copyright royalties.
The agreement contains the usual rule, adopted by all the members of the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development, that the industrial or commercial profits of an enterprise of one of the countries shall be taxed in the other country only if the enterprise has a permanent establishment in that other country and only to the extent that they are attributable to that permanent establishment. This exempts a taxpayer of one country from taxation in the other country, if he merely buys goods there. It also protects a taxpayer who only sells goods in the other country through an independent agent or an agent who merely takes orders and does not conclude contracts.
The agreement provides that the profits of an enterprise from the operation of ships or aircraft in international traffic shall be taxable only where the enterprise is resident. This provision is similar to that in most other agreements.
April 26, 1966

The agreement provides that copyright royalties and similar payments in respect of the use of literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work, not including royalties for motion picture or television films, shall be exempt from tax in the country of source. Canada exempts such payments to non-residents in its Income Tax Act but, following the termination of the old agreement, Britain has been imposing its standard 41J per cent tax on these royalties paid from sources in Britain to Canadian residents. Persons in Canada who receive such royalties will thus obtain relief.
The provisions of the agreement are designed to come into operation on the dates the old agreement ceased to have effect. For Canada this will be January 1, 1965 and taxation years ending in or after 1965. Refunds will be made where taxes contrary to the new agreement have been levied during the period from the date of the termination of the old agreement to the date of the coming into force of the new agreement.
The new agreement will come into force after each contracting government has been notified that all the things that have to be done to give the agreement the force of law in Canada and the United Kingdom respectively have been done. The government of the United Kingdom has notified the government of Canada that it has completed the necessary actions. The agreement will accordingly come into force when the royal assent is given to this bill.
Part II of the bill deals with the supplementary agreement between Canada and Sweden. The purpose of the supplementary agreement is to make several amendments to the income tax agreement between Canada and Sweden signed in 1951. The change of most importance for Canada is the deletion of a provision that prevents a non-resident withholding tax of more than 5 per cent controlled subsidiary company in one of the countries to its parent company in the other. Each country continues to agree not to impose a withholding tax on dividends in excess of 15 per cent. The normal rate imposed by Sweden when there is no tax agreement is 30 per cent. This change will bring the Cana-da-Sweden agreement into conformity with the announced policy of the Canadian government.
The supplementary agreement will come into force on the date when the exchange of instruments of ratification takes place, and
Income Tax
will be effective in Canada for the taxation year 1966 and subsequent taxation years. The effective date for the replacement of the 5 per cent maximum withholding rate by the 15 per cent maximum withholding rate on certain dividends will be April 1, 1966. I am hopeful that the supplementary agreement will enter into force before many more weeks have passed.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to see that the government of Canada has come forward with this particular bill, because we were getting more and more anguished cries, and I think legitimate ones, from many Canadians who were holding investments in British concerns-and this of course is something which is to be encouraged. Canadians do hold interests in operations abroad, but since 1964 of course they were subject to the penalties of double taxation. This frankly does not enhance our attractiveness to British investment in Canada or to Canadian investment abroad. There certainly is no incentive to Canadian coporations to establish operations in the United Kingdom. Not only does this have an effect on the industrial and business field, but it has an effect on the thousands upon thousands of new Canadians-that is an odd term-of British origin who settled here after world war II. Many of them are veterans and are entitled to service pensions, either for reasons of disability or otherwise, yet they are very seriously penalized. The fact that they could take their pensions and come to Canada under the former tax agreement was one of the major considerations which led them to come here in the first place.
Because Canada was in some difficulty regarding the high rate of withholding tax in relation to British operations in Canada, this agreement was cast aside and allowed to lapse. This came about as one of the unfortunate consequences of the budget of 1963, and some of the things that followed.
I agree that there may be some argument that Canada should not be prepared to enter into a finite agreement pending the Carter commission on taxation, in view of the fact that Britain has also made some rather drastic changes in its structure, and we may expect more; but as an investor I would find it rather difficult to forecast the future, certainly in respect of long-term investments in growth stocks, and I would not be encouraged by the interim nature of this agreement.

April 26. 1966
Income Tax
By reason of article XI the whole agreement may be terminated by Canada effectively with six months' notice, and by the United Kingdom in a matter of a little more than nine months because of its tax year. Why Britain insists on retaining April 6 as the date on which it collects revenue I do not know, but in my opinion one of the negative aspects is this agreement not being made for a finite period.
With that reservation I earnestly hope that before long the government will have studied the Carter report on taxation and made up its mind on what it intends to do with regard to taxation. I hope there will not be any undue delay either on the part of the government whether this one or one formed by the opposition, in allowing the implementation of the major recommendations of that commission's report. I hope that a finite agreement can be reached expeditiously at that time.
Any further remarks I wish to make can be made more appropriately when we are considering the bill clause by clause. Once again I wish to say that I find the omnibus clauses too all-encompassing. I refer particularly to clause 2(3) which provides that-
-the Minister of National Revenue may make such orders and regulations as are. in his opinion, necessary for the purpose of carrying out the agreement or for giving effect to any of the provisions thereof.
I do not know how many times I have said that I am overly suspicious of such clauses. Administrative regulations which embody matters of policy ought first to be considered by the house, but they often find their way into legislation through a back door. For this reason I return to the point made by the committee on procedure, that there should be a committee of this house to review delegated powers. When the minister creates any regulation under the powers granted to him by *clause 2(3) he should be required to come before the parliament to satisfy that body that he has not exceeded his powers or created any regulation the effect of which is retroactive to the authorization of those powers.
I urge the minister to refer this recommendation to his colleagues-because this is one of the more serious aspects that we should consider-so that regulations do not become pseudo-legislation by means of regulatory powers.
